sweep_summary: Single works with stress in the title, Robbins 1991 'Lexicalized Metrical Foot Structure in Maidu' (PASC 2:95-116), is squarely about Northeast Maidu word stress and is the primary origin (with Hayes 1995:261) of the CVC-heavy initial/second-syllable rule the catalog carries via StressTyp2; it remains unobtainable online: UCSC's Linguistics Research Center page confirms PASC vol. 2 (Mester & Robbins eds., 1991, vii+116 pp., paper, no ISBN) is print-only with no eScholarship copy (only vols 6-7 are digitized), Google Books holds the 1991 volume with no page view (id EsZwAAAAIAAJ), and Crossref/Semantic Scholar/archive.org have no record; Hayes 1995 (Google Books id ST1JpDcrR3sC) could not be searched inside (captcha). Dixon's 1911 Maidu sketch in Boas's Handbook (already held by the project), Phonetics sections 2-4 pp. 684-687, says nothing about stress placement. No new first-hand stress statement was read; the catalog's deciding source (Shipley 1964, page-image) stands. Acquisition priority for Robbins 1991: high (ILL from a library holding PASC 2, or request from UCSC LRC / sasc@ucsc.edu).

audit.reasoning: Quote check passes: every fragment of the deciding quotation is verbatim in the held Shipley 1964 scanned/page scan at the cited pages (6, 10-11, 21, 22; Sect.321 p.16 too). The deciding source is the standard reference grammar and nothing newer or instrumental on Maidu stress surfaced (CrossRef, archive.org; Glottolog's list has no later grammar or phonology). The record is honest about the split: Shipley = phonemic/lexical stress with root-shape tendencies; the CVC-heavy I/S;I rule is a Robbins 1991/Hayes 1995 reanalysis reached only through StressTyp2, and StressTyp2's 'Shipley 1964:13' passage is a paraphrase not found in Shipley. Hence 'weight-hedged' is the right call and not at risk, but the weight half rests on two unheld theoretical sources; obtaining Robbins 1991 (high) or Hayes 1995:261 (medium) and re-reading would let the record quote the rule from its actual author and report

sources.note: Shipley's own analysis: three phonemic stress degrees (primary /´/, secondary /`/, weak unmarked). Stress is lexical/morphemic: the root morph carries the stress morphophoneme ||´|| as part of its shape (sec. 500; roots are 'at least one segmental syllable along with ||´|| or ||.´||'), a class of 'delayed-stress' roots (||mo.´||) puts it on the syllable following the root segments. Primary vs secondary is positional: within the domain bounded by junctures (+.) or silence the FIRST stress is primary and every later stress is demoted to secondary (sec. 321). Examples show root stress on initi

sources.access_detail: open copy posted by the author (located 2026-09-25); a digital copy (available on request)
sources.quote: All roots have at least one allomorph which occurs with primary stress. If the root is disyllabic, the primary stress is on the first syllable in some words, the second syllable in others. In compound words (i.e., in words which are made up of more than one root) one of the roots has primary stress while the others have a secondary stress. The primary stress may appear on the first member of the compound in one instance, on the second in another, and so on. In short, stress is phonemic. The primary stress is characterized by: (a) relatively fortis enunciation; (b) a pitch about one tone higher than the pitches of the adjacent syllables; (c) about two morae of length in the stressed vowel, if the syllable is open. The secondary stress is characterized by: (a) relatively fortis enunciation; (b) about two morae of length in the stressed vowel, if the syllable is open. There is no difference in pitch between syllables with secondary stress and syllables without stress. Vowels in closed syllables are never more than one mora in length, no matter what the nature of the stress may be.
